correctness.rationale: All quantified variables are explicit: n>=3 and integer 3<=k<=n, uniform permutations. Three mutually exclusive first-partner arrival cases have exact probabilities 1-1/n, (n-2)/[2n(2n-1)], and q_n=3/[2(2n-1)]. In the regenerative branch, removing the closed matching pair leaves a uniform smaller crown order and shifts all its colors by one, including when exactly one opposite-side vertex appeared first. This proves the tail recursion, closed product, factorial extremal count and expectation expansion by induction and tail bounds. The n=2 boundary is handled. Packaged Python verification directly enumerates n<=4 orders and exactly sums all (2n)! orders by memoized prefix-color states through n=7, matching rational predictions. Computations corroborate rather than replace the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The initiating work arXiv:2608.29603v1 (2026-08-30), Section 3.1, Theorem 3, establishes only an expectation upper bound 2.5+O(1/n) on the identical random-order crown graph. Its complete accessible HTML including the theorem and proof was inspected. It neither states an exact color-count distribution nor determines a limit of 2, a full tail, or the factorial worst-case probability. Targeted searches for random-order FirstFit/Grundy equivalences, exact tables, and published mathematical-record comparisons returned no covering result. Prior work on forests, adversarial coloring, and random greedy independent sets does not imply this law; however unindexed earlier probabilistic Grundy literature is a residual risk.

value.rationale: Crown graphs exhibit an unbounded ratio of adversarial FirstFit colors n to chromatic number 2, motivating the recently studied random-order regime. The current literature gives an upper mean bound of 2.5+O(1/n). The full law exactly quantifies every tail, the rare worst-case coloring probability, and improves the asymptotic mean to 2+1/n+3/(4n^2)+O(n^-3). It supplies a regenerative mechanism and a natural quantitative benchmark for random-order online coloring, not a numerical recomputation or an arbitrarily chosen parameter slice. The all-n classification makes the result useful independent of broader conjectures.
